shock: Congo cobalt export quota (96.6 kt a year incl. 9.6 kt reserve, CMOC entitlement 31.2 kt of 117.5 kt)
affected_families: Superalloy bar, billet and remelt stock (Co bearing grades); CoCr bar and powder (Co about 60 percent)
gap_or_exposure: Mine supply 2035 225 kt base, 206 kt with quota held (gap 36 percent of IEA Stated Policies demand, base 30), 147 kt at CMOC entitlement ratio (gap 54 percent). Model superalloy cobalt 2035 P50 25.6 kt = 11 percent of base supply, 17 percent in the tight case. Alloy grade metal is about 15 kt a year from four refiners outside the hydroxide chain (Cobalt Institute).
cost_effect: Pass through by surcharge or alloy price, lagged, qualitative: no surcharge table is in the repository (TODO(data)). Team arithmetic: at 8 percent virgin cobalt a tonne of superalloy holds 176 lb Co, worth USD 3,704 at USD 21 per lb (2025 estimate), so the 25 percent price rise from USD 16.77 (2024) adds about USD 746 per tonne. For CoCr (about 600 kg Co per tonne) the same move adds about USD 5,595. Fixed price long term agreements keep the risk with the melter.

shock: China tungsten export licence halt (licence regime since 4 February 2025, APT, oxide, unsintered carbide)
affected_families: Flat products and bar in C-276 and C-22 type grades (W about 4 and 3 percent); tungsten bearing cast and wrought superalloys (content TODO(data))
gap_or_exposure: Ex China mine supply 2025 = 85,000 t minus 67,000 t = 18,000 t contained tungsten (21 percent of world). Each 10 kt of C-276 uses 0.4 kt W = 2.2 percent of ex China mine supply. No tungsten tonnes to 2035 exist (TODO(data)), so no gap is computed. Sintered carbide and wire are outside the licence.
cost_effect: Tungsten is priced by surcharge or in the alloy price. Team arithmetic: 40 kg W per tonne of C-276 is 5.04 mtu WO3, which cost USD 1,271 at the 2024 concentrate price (USD 252) and USD 1,917 at the 2025 price (USD 380), an increase of USD 646 per tonne. Another doubling would add about USD 1,917 per tonne, about 5.9 percent of the German export unit value of USD 32,500 per tonne for nickel flat (concentrate basis, metal costs more).
tier_effect: no tier changes; score moves: Chemical plate, welding wire 2.55 to 2.40; Alloy C-276 fusion tape foil 2.75 to 2.60
score_moves_without_tier_change: Chemical plate, welding wire 2.55 to 2.40; Alloy C-276 fusion tape foil 2.75 to 2.60

shock: Indonesia nickel ore quota cut (RKAB 2026 revised -22 percent, initial -29 percent, Weda Bay style -71 percent)
affected_families: All nickel alloy families, first through the nickel price; class 1 alloy feed is mostly outside Indonesian NPI
gap_or_exposure: Mine supply 2035 gap 6.5 percent of IEA Stated Policies demand in the base case, 21.4 percent at -22 percent, 26.7 percent at -29 percent, 54.6 percent at -71 percent. The primary refined gap is already 20.6 percent.
cost_effect: Pass through by the monthly alloy surcharge on lagged LME nickel, molybdenum and chromium averages, so margin is exposed only on fixed price contracts and inventory. ATI: nickel use about 70 million lb, so USD 1.00 per lb is about USD 70 m of cost, mostly passed through (CO_ATI_SALES_2025). Team arithmetic: USD 1,000 per tonne on LME nickel adds about USD 10 per tonne of alloy for every percentage point of nickel content.

shock: Severe aerospace demand case: two years at minus 20 percent (2026 and 2027), then recovery (motivated by 2020)
affected_families: Superalloy bar, billet and remelt stock (aerospace weight 0.575), engine bar and billet
gap_or_exposure: Aerospace 2035 index P10/P50/P90: base 121/136/151. Severe with 70 percent recovery 96/114/133, no recovery of the lost level 77/87/96. Superalloy family P50 129 to 116. Aviation cobalt 2035 P50 15.4 to 13.0 kt. Cumulative metal demand 2026 to 2035 on the P50 path is 22.5 percent below base.
cost_effect: Not a supply shock: volume loss. Mills with fixed capital in VIM and VAR lose utilisation. Backlogs (Airbus 8,754 aircraft, Boeing more than 6,300) and engine shop visits cushion the aftermarket half of the index.
